hints: Look at where V sits in the diagram - it is in one of the two small circular vessels below the main heart mass, not between an atrium and a ventricle, so think about which set of valves guards the exits from the ventricles.
walkthrough:
Locate V in the Heart Plan**
The section is just above the valves. The two large chambers at the top are the atria and ventricles in section, and the two small circles below are the aorta and pulmonary artery leaving the ventricles. V is guarding the exit from a ventricle into a great artery.

Name the Exit Valve**
Valves between ventricles and the aorta or pulmonary artery that prevent backflow into the ventricles are the semilunar valves. V is therefore a semilunar valve, either the aortic or the pulmonary valve.
Final answer: Semilunar valve (aortic valve or pulmonary valve).

hints: Compare Fig. 3.1 with Fig. 3.2 - in Fig. 3.1 the large upper valves are open and V below is closed, so think about which direction blood can move when the route between upper chambers is open but the exit to the arteries is shut.
Remember blood is always entering the atria from the great veins, so think about which veins fill the left atrium and which veins fill the right atrium while the atria are emptying downwards.
walkthrough:
Read the Valve State in Fig. 3.1**
In Fig. 3.1 the atrioventricular valves at the top are open and the semilunar valves including V are closed. That means there is no exit from the ventricles to the arteries, but there is an open passage downwards.

Follow the Blood Path**
With the atrioventricular valves open, pressure from the atria pushes blood down from atria to ventricles. This is atrial systole with relaxed ventricles. At the same time blood continues to arrive into the atria: into the left atrium from the pulmonary vein and into the right atrium from the vena cava (superior and inferior venae cavae).
Final answer: Blood flows from the atria to the ventricles; blood flows into the left and right atria from the pulmonary vein and vena cava.

hints: Look carefully at Fig. 3.2 - the upper valves now show closed flaps meeting in the middle while the two small lower vessels are wide open, so think about which contraction would need to shut the upper route and force open the lower route.
Link high pressure in the contracting chamber to valve action - think about what high ventricular pressure does to the atrioventricular valves below and to the semilunar valves above.
walkthrough:
Decode Fig. 3.2**
The atrioventricular valves are shut with their cusps pressed together, while the semilunar valves in the aorta and pulmonary artery are open as wide circles. That is the opposite of Fig. 3.1.

Match to Ventricular Systole**
When the thick ventricular muscle contracts, ventricular pressure rises above atrial and arterial pressure. This slams the atrioventricular valves shut to prevent backflow to the atria and forces the semilunar valves open so blood is ejected into the aorta and pulmonary artery. This combination only occurs in ventricular systole.
Final answer: Stage: ventricular systole; Reason: atrioventricular (bicuspid/mitral and tricuspid) valves are closed and semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves are open.

hints: Start from the sinoatrial node in the right atrium wall - after it fires and the atria contract, the wave of excitation cannot pass directly through the non-conducting septum, so think about where the impulse must be picked up next.
Think about timing - think why the ventricles must wait about 0.1 s after the atria start to contract and what useful filling or emptying this delay allows.
Think about the path that lets the ventricles contract from the bottom up - think about which fibres carry the impulse rapidly down the septum to the apex and then spread it upwards.
walkthrough:
AVN Pickup and Delay**
Excitation spreading across the atria reaches the atrioventricular node between the atria. The impulse is held for a short delay of about 0.1 s. This is vital because it lets the atria finish contracting and empty fully into the ventricles, so atria and ventricles do not contract at the same time and ventricles are fully filled.

Rapid Conduction to the Apex**
The atrioventricular node then passes the impulse into the bundle of His and Purkyne (Purkinje) fibres running down through the septum. These conducting fibres carry the impulse very fast to the base or apex of the ventricles.

Coordinated Upward Contraction**
From the apex the impulse spreads upwards through ventricular muscle. This makes both ventricles contract at the same time, squeezing from the base upwards, which pushes blood efficiently up into the aorta and pulmonary artery.

Final answer: Impulses from SAN reach the atrioventricular node where there is a short delay of about 0.1 s, allowing atria to complete contraction and ventricles to fill; AVN sends impulses down the bundle of His and Purkyne fibres to the base/apex of ventricles, then upwards, causing both ventricles to contract together from base upwards.
